summary: Children (age 7-8) learn to draw 2-D shapes accurately, build 3-D solids from modelling materials, and recognise a 3-D shape as the same shape when it is rotated or seen from a new angle. Two procedural strands matter: constructing a solid correctly requires coordinating its edge/vertex/face structure (a cube has 12 equal edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and orientation recognition requires naming a shape by properties that stay the same under rotation. The central obstacle is orientation dependence: a child anchored to a canonical view judges a rotated or point-down solid to be 'a different shape'. The curriculum calls for making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so hands-on building, rotating real solids, and careful drawing on dotted paper/geoboards are the core activities; on-screen builders and spinners are useful complements, and recognition tasks can check outcomes but do not by themselves elicit construction.
misconceptions: Does not recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — calls a rotated or point-down pyramid 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or with the wrong number of sides.
Treats a shape's name as tied to its usual position, so turning it seems to change what it is.

activities.title: Build a cube frame from straws and connectors
steps: Before building, predict and count how many edges (straws) and vertices (connectors) a cube needs, and state the target: 12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces.
Build the cube frame, snapping straws (edges) onto connectors (balls of clay or plastic joints for vertices).

Check that every straw is the same length and that the corners are square (right angles, not leaning), because equal straws alone can still give a squashed frame with diamond-shaped faces; then compare the finished frame against a real cube-shaped solid.
Point to and count the edges, vertices and faces on the completed frame to confirm the structure.
Try building a cuboid with edges of different lengths as a contrast and describe how it differs from the cube (not all edges equal, so some faces are rectangles that are not squares).
activities.insight: A cube is defined by its structure — 12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces — and building it requires coordinating that structure rather than approximating a box shape.

activities.title: Rotate a solid and keep naming it
steps: Hold a real pyramid (or cube) and physically turn it: point-up, on its side, point-down, and viewed from directly above.
At each orientation, say what the shape is and how you know, naming it by its properties (e.g. 'a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex').
State explicitly whether the name changed when the shape turned, and explain why it should not.
Repeat with a cuboid laid on different faces, confirming it is the same solid each time.
activities.insight: A shape's name comes from properties that do not change when it is rotated or viewed from a new angle; turning a solid does not make it a different shape.

activities.title: Draw 2-D shapes accurately on dotted paper or a geoboard
steps: Draw named 2-D shapes (triangle, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon) on dotted paper or a geoboard.
Count and mark each side as it is drawn, keeping track so the figure closes with the right number of straight sides.
After drawing, re-count the sides and check the shape is closed and has straight (not curved) edges.
Draw the same shape again at a different size and confirm it keeps its name (a bigger hexagon is still a hexagon).
activities.insight: An accurate 2-D shape is a closed figure with the correct number of straight sides; its name depends on properties such as closure, side count and, for shapes like rectangles, right angles, not on size.

activities.title: Link nets and faces to the built solid
steps: Fold a net into a solid, then identify each face as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
For a built cube frame, point out where each square face sits between four edges.
Match the faces on the net to the faces on the solid, naming the 2-D shape of each (square, triangle).
activities.insight: Each face of a solid is a 2-D shape, so 2-D and 3-D shape knowledge connect: a cube's faces are squares, a pyramid's faces include triangles.

activities.title: On-screen builder and spinner (complementary digital practice)
steps: Using a construction tool, snap virtual edges onto vertices to build a cube; watch a live tally of edges, vertices and faces update as you work.
Notice that a lopsided attempt with unequal edges does not resolve into a correct cube until the structure matches 12 edges, 8 vertices and six square faces.
Grab and spin an on-screen pyramid through point-up, on-its-side, point-down and top-down views, reading a label that continues to name it 'a pyramid' in every orientation.
Where possible, pair each on-screen task with the matching physical build or real solid so the hands confirm the screen.
activities.insight: A live edge/vertex/face tally and free rotation make the structure and its invariance under rotation visible; the digital model complements, and does not replace, handling real solids.

checkQuestion: Set three tasks and watch: (1) 'Draw a hexagon as accurately as you can.' (2) 'Build a cube using these straws and connectors.' (3) Show a pyramid, then rotate it — lay it on its side, stand it point-down, show it from directly above — asking each time: 'Is this still the same shape? What is it?'
checkAnswer: (1) A closed, six-sided, straight-edged figure. (2) A cube built from 12 equal straws (edges) and 8 connectors (vertices), giving 6 square faces. (3) Identifies it as the same pyramid in every orientation — a shape's name does not change when it is rotated or viewed from a different angle.
